name: Turmeric / gram flour hair removal paste

lead: Ubtan is a traditional herbal formulation from the Indian system of medicine, commonly made from gram (chickpea) flour and turmeric among other ingredients, and used on the skin. Folk use extends to rubbing the dried paste off to lift fine body hair.
Research located covers ubtan as a skin-care preparation. No published study found tested whether it removes or reduces hair.

paras: Proponents describe it as a gentle abrasive and plant-based mixture that rubs fine hair away and, with repeated use, thins regrowth. This mechanism has not been tested in published human studies.
No safety data specific to hair removal were found. Turmeric is known to stain skin and fabric, and topical plant preparations can in general cause irritation or allergic reactions.

studies.title: Evaluation of Ubtan - A traditional indian skin care formulation.

lead: Turmeric and gram flour pastes are folk preparations associated with ubtan, a traditional herbal skin-care formulation used in India and the surrounding region for a long time and now also sold as commercial products under the same name.[1] Home versions are described by practitioners as a way to remove fine body hair or slow its regrowth.

A 2016 Journal of Ethnopharmacology study prepared ubtan and standardised it using chromatographic techniques, evaluating it as a skin-care formulation.[1] No published study located tested the paste for hair removal, so its use for that purpose rests on traditional practice.

paras: Ubtan is a traditional herbal formulation of the Indian system of medicine, used for skin care across the Indian subcontinent for a long time, and several commercial skin products carry the name.[1] The hair-removal variant usually mixes gram flour and turmeric into a paste that is applied and then rubbed off once dry; the practice is described here at a general level only.
Practitioners of the folk method say the paste lifts fine hair and, with repeated use, reduces regrowth. No source located tested these claims.

No studies found. The closest research is a 2016 laboratory study that prepared and standardised ubtan using chromatographic techniques and evaluated it as a skin-care formulation, not as a hair remover.[1]
